blocks.html: Five fights back to back with one fixed team: Moleman, Elias, Arabella and Penny in any order, then Champion Jax. On Expert every one of them brings six fully EV'd mons, legendaries included. Their mons are Lv 74 to 76 against your cap of 75.

How this chapter was built. Rosters are the Expert sets (nuzlockeredux for moves and abilities; held items from the Unbound Wiki on Miraheze where shown). Every damage number is a Showdown calc estimate at Lv 75 with the boss's listed nature and EVs where known, otherwise assuming 252 in its attacking stat. Your moves are checked against Unbound's learnset files and TM list.
What you'll do: five fights back to back with one fixed six and no Pokémon Center: Moleman, Elias, Arabella and Penny (any order), then Champion Jax.
Your six: Mamoswine, Garchomp, Houndoom, Metagross, Gardevoir, Togekiss.
Recommended order: Moleman, Elias, Arabella, Penny, then Jax.

items.html: Before you walk in: League six at 75 with EVs and natures done, and spare held items in your bag. Items can be swapped between rooms; the table further down says who holds what in each room.
Pick up four free Max Ethers at the Magnolia Café. PP runs low by the time you reach Jax.
Fight in the recommended order. Each fight has its own red short-version box.
Heal between rooms, not mid-fight. You still only get four items per battle.
No team changes between fights. No Porta-PC.
You can swap held items between rooms, so bring spares and re-equip for each opponent (table below).
Four bag items per battle, so heal between rooms, not mid-fight.
Bosses use Full Restores when a mon is in KO range (Unbound Wiki's counts: Moleman 2, Elias 1, Arabella 2, Penny 2, Jax 3; those are Vanilla figures). Finish targets in one go rather than chipping.
One Mega per battle. Your four Mega Stones are spread across the six, so you pick the Mega for each room by who holds a stone.
PP runs low by Jax (Unbound Wiki). Magnolia Café gives four free Max Ethers.

blocks.html: Recommended order: Moleman, Elias, Arabella, Penny, then Jax. Moleman first while Mamoswine and Garchomp are fresh and you have the most PP; Elias second because Mega Houndoom solos most of it; Arabella third because Mega Metagross does the same there; Penny last before Jax so your Gardevoir and Togekiss doubles plan is warmed up for the same plan against Jax.

Greninja (Protean, Specs) and Mega Absol are both reasonable alternatives in some rooms, but I haven't re-run the five fights with them, so the plans and calcs below assume this six.

blocks.html: Why it's hard: two Sand Rush attackers move first in a sandstorm you can't remove, Earthquake and Rock Slide hit both your mons every turn, and Landorus-T and Gliscor dodge Ground moves.
Lead: Mamoswine + Togekiss. Mega: Garchomp. Back: Garchomp, Gardevoir (Specs), Metagross, Houndoom.
Damage you can count on:
Turn by turn

items.html: Turn 1 (likely leads Excadrill + Flygon): Mamoswine Icicle Crash Flygon (OHKO, before Throat Spray goes off). Togekiss Air Slash Excadrill to break the Focus Sash (resisted, but any damage breaks it), or Follow Me if you'd rather protect Mamoswine from Iron Head. If Excadrill Protects, Togekiss's hit is wasted; repeat next turn. If Excadrill Iron Heads Mamoswine first (it's only 5 Speed points slower, so a speed tie on rounding can go either way), Mamoswine may drop. Max Revive it next turn only if the field is clear; otherwise bring Garchomp.

Turn 2: Mamoswine Earthquake (Togekiss is immune). Excadrill dies with the Sash gone, and Sandslash or Quagsire on the field take a chunk. Scarf locks Mamoswine into Earthquake: that's fine while Togekiss is the partner.

Gliscor and Landorus-T (Ground/Flying): Earthquake does nothing; you're locked into it, so switch Mamoswine out and back in to pick Icicle Crash (4x). Landorus-T's Intimidate hits on entry: Icicle Crash still does 79 to 96% at -1, so follow with Ice Shard or Togekiss's Air Slash.
Quagsire (Water Absorb, Yawn, Recover): bring in Gardevoir with Specs and Energy Ball (OHKO). If Yawn hits something, switch that mon out before it falls asleep.
Sandslash: Mega Garchomp's Sand Force Earthquake (61 to 71%, spread) or Icicle Crash.
Mega Garchomp cleans up. Mega Evolve it the first turn it's out; Sand Force powers its Earthquake, Rock and Steel moves. Keep it next to Togekiss so the spread hits nothing of yours.

blocks.html: Watch out

items.html: Houndoom and Metagross are both weak to Ground. Keep them in the back. Metagross can come in on Rock Slide; Houndoom shouldn't come in at all.
Gliscor's Sand Veil makes it dodge 20% of the time. If Icicle Crash misses, Ice Shard is the backup.
Backup plan: if Mamoswine goes down early, Gardevoir (Specs Energy Ball on Quagsire, Shadow Ball elsewhere) and Mega Garchomp can carry, with Togekiss redirecting Rock Slides with Follow Me.

blocks.html: Expect the switch: this is a double battle, and in the engine's switching code the "dodge an OHKO" switch only exists in single battles. So Mamoswine's Icicle Crash on Flygon should land rather than make him swap. What the AI does do in doubles is bring in a mon that absorbs your attack, and swap out a mon whose moves are all useless against both of yours. Here that means:

items.html: Water moves get soaked by Quagsire (Water Absorb). Don't use any while it's alive.

Earthquake can't touch Flygon, Gliscor or Landorus-T, but the doubles AI won't switch them in just for that (type immunities aren't part of its absorb check). Just don't aim Earthquake into a slot where one of them already stands.

If he does pull Flygon anyway (Unbound's build isn't public, so you could be right), nothing on his team resists Ice. Whatever comes in still takes a neutral Icicle Crash, which costs him a mon's worth of HP for nothing.

blocks.html: Lead Metagross: Bullet Punch breaks Mimikyu's Disguise, Meteor Mash kills it. Then Mega Houndoom solos most of it: Dark Pulse or Flamethrower. Kill Cofagrigus before it Iron Defenses twice; Gardevoir's Specs Shadow Ball is the backup.

blocks.title: Elite Four Elias
meta: Shadowy Veil: his Ghosts take reduced damage at full HP and ignore hazards at full HP; Substitute and Safeguard fail for your non-Ghosts

mons.label: Mimikyu
fields: Jolly. +2 Play Rough does 82 to 97% to Mega Houndoom

mons.name: Cofagrigus
mons.label: Cofagrigus

blocks.html: Lead: Metagross (Leftovers) for Mimikyu. Mega: Houndoom. Back: Garchomp (Life Orb) as the Blacephalon backup, Gardevoir (Specs) for Cofagrigus.
Damage you can count on (before the field's full-HP damage cut, which roughly halves the first hit on each of his mons):
Turn by turn

items.html: Lead Metagross against Mimikyu. Bullet Punch breaks Disguise (and takes it off full HP, so the field stops shielding it). Next turn, Meteor Mash kills it. Metagross resists Play Rough, but Shadow Claw and Shadow Sneak are 2x on it, so don't hang around. If Mimikyu Swords Dances on turn 1, that's fine: break Disguise, then kill it before it attacks twice.
Switch to Houndoom and Mega Evolve. Mega Houndoom (about 272 Speed) is just faster than a Timid max-Speed Blacephalon (about 263).

Aegislash: Dark Pulse or Flamethrower (2x each), ideally right after it attacks (Blade form). It takes two hits in Shield form. Toxic still lands on Houndoom; Metagross is immune if you need to switch.
Trevenant: Flamethrower (98 to 117%). Houndoom resists both its attacks and can't be burned.

Cofagrigus: kill it before it uses Iron Defense twice. Once it's at +2, Body Press OHKOs Mega Houndoom. Dark Pulse does 82 to 96% (less on the shielded first hit), so expect two hits; if it Iron Defenses on turn 1, it's already +1, so switch to Gardevoir (Specs Shadow Ball, 2x and special) rather than risk it. Never touch it with contact moves: Mummy overwrites your ability.

Banette: Dark Pulse (75% OHKO). If it's low, watch Destiny Bond: with Prankster it goes first and takes your attacker down with it. Destiny Bond fails if used twice in a row, so hit it the turn after, or finish it with a mon you can spare.

Blacephalon: Houndoom resists Flamethrower and Shadow Ball and is immune to Psyshock. Expect two Dark Pulses because of the full-HP shield. If it holds Weakness Policy (one wiki says so), the first hit gives it +2, but its moves still barely touch Houndoom. If it has Hidden Power Fighting (one older listing), that's 2x on Houndoom: switch to Garchomp, which resists Flamethrower, and Earthquake it (223 to 262%).

blocks.html: Watch out: Gardevoir is weak to Ghost; keep it in for one Shadow Ball, not a slugfest.

Expect the switch: single battle, so he can dodge, but he has nothing to dodge into. Every mon he has is a Ghost, so Dark Pulse is super effective on all of them, and Blacephalon (the only one that resists Fire) is slower than Mega Houndoom and can't take a Dark Pulse. The AI only switches to something that walls you, is immune, or outspeeds and KOs you, so expect him to stay in and trade. Metagross versus Mimikyu is the same story: Mimikyu is faster, and a faster mon never switches to dodge.

Mega Metagross's Meteor Mash kills Ribombee, Sylveon and Togekiss. Gardevoir's Specs Energy Ball for Azumarill and Tapu Fini, Houndoom's Flamethrower for Mega Mawile. Keep Garchomp out: every Fairy move is 2x on it.

meta: Misty Terrain all fight (no status on grounded mons, Dragon moves weakened); her Fairies get +1 to their weaker defence when they switch in

Damage you can count on (her mons at +1 Defence on switch-in where Defence is their weaker side):
Turn by turn

items.html: Ribombee leads and is faster than Mega Metagross, so expect Sticky Web or a screen first. Mega Evolve and Meteor Mash (OHKO). Sticky Web only slows mons that switch in, so the longer Metagross stays in, the better.
Sylveon: Meteor Mash (OHKO). You're faster.

Togekiss: Meteor Mash (OHKO). A Metagross that switched in on Sticky Web is slower than a max-Speed Togekiss, and then Air Slash flinches 60% of the time: in that case use Scarf Mamoswine's Icicle Crash (2x) instead.
Azumarill: Gardevoir's Specs Energy Ball (84 to 99%). Mega Metagross also takes only 36 to 43% from Aqua Tail, so it can trade with Meteor Mash if it has to.
Mega Mawile: Intimidate hits on entry, so answer with special Fire: Houndoom's Flamethrower (OHKO). Houndoom resists Iron Head and Sucker Punch.

Tapu Fini is the slow grind: Nature's Madness takes half your HP each time and Taunt stops healing. Gardevoir's Energy Ball (49 to 59%) plus a Meteor Mash finishes it. Its Surf is 2x on Houndoom and Mamoswine is neutral.

blocks.html: Watch out: Garchomp takes 2x from every Fairy move and its Dragon moves do nothing to Fairies: it never comes in here.

Expect the switch: probably a single battle, but Mega Metagross has nothing to fear: nothing on her team resists Steel (Steel is 2x on Fairy, and even Mega Mawile only takes it neutral), and nothing outspeeds and OHKOs Mega Metagross. Two spots where she can switch:

items.html: Houndoom's Flamethrower on Mega Mawile: Azumarill or Tapu Fini (both resist Fire) can come in to take it. If one does, switch to Gardevoir for Energy Ball.
Gardevoir's Energy Ball on Azumarill: Togekiss, Ribombee and Mega Mawile all resist Grass. If one comes in, Meteor Mash it next turn; it can't switch again straight away.

blocks.html: Double battle. Togekiss uses Follow Me, Gardevoir Mega Evolves and spams Hyper Voice. That kills Tyrantrum, Goodra, Kommo-o and Hydreigon. Scarf Mamoswine's Icicle Crash for Mega Sceptile and Latias. Don't Earthquake unless Togekiss is your partner.

mons.name: Tyrantrum

Damage you can count on:
Turn by turn

items.html: Turn 1 (leads Goodra + Tyrantrum, as listed): Togekiss Follow Me. Gardevoir Mega Evolves and Hyper Voices: Tyrantrum dies, Goodra takes 59 to 71%. Tyrantrum's Iron Head and Goodra's Sludge Bomb go into Togekiss (Iron Head 37 to 44%; Togekiss is Fairy/Flying, so Sludge Bomb is 2x on it too: it can take one, then Roost).
Turn 2: Hyper Voice again finishes Goodra and hits whatever came in. Togekiss Follow Me again, or Dazzling Gleam for extra spread damage if nothing threatens Gardevoir.
Kommo-o and Hydreigon both die to one Hyper Voice. Hydreigon sets Tailwind if it gets a turn: kill it on sight.
Mega Sceptile: Hyper Voice (2x), or Scarf Mamoswine's Icicle Crash (4x).
Latias: Mist Ball cuts the Sp. Atk of whatever it hits, every time, so finish it physically: Scarf Mamoswine's Icicle Crash (94% OHKO). It has Roost; don't chip it.
Paralysis: Dragon Breath paralyses 60% of the time. Cure with Full Heals between rooms; in battle, only if the paralysed mon is Gardevoir.

blocks.html: Watch out

items.html: Don't Earthquake in this room unless Togekiss is the partner.
Tyrantrum's High Horsepower is 2x on Metagross and Houndoom; they stay back until it's gone.
Backup plan: if Togekiss falls early, put Metagross next to Gardevoir: it resists Dragon, Rock and Steel and can take the Iron Heads.

blocks.html: Expect the switch: double battle, so no dodge-an-OHKO switching. Watch for absorbers: Mega Sceptile's Lightning Rod pulls in every Electric move (don't use any), (Lightning Rod also redirects them while it's on the field). Hydreigon and Latias are immune to Earthquake through Levitate, but that's not something the AI switches in for, so just aim Earthquake at the other slot. Your Fairy, Ice and Steel attacks have no absorbers on her side.

Double battle. Togekiss Follow Me, Mega Gardevoir Hyper Voice turn 1 kills Mega Salamence. If Hitmontop Wide Guards, Psyshock it. Kill Hitmontop early, keep Mamoswine and Garchomp back until both Intimidates are spent, and kill Naganadel before Beast Boost snowballs.

mons.name: Mega Salamence
mons.label: Mega Salamence
fields: Faster than Mega Gardevoir; Double-Edge OHKOs her (146 to 172%)

mons.name: Naganadel
mons.label: Naganadel
fields: Sludge Bomb does 83 to 98% to Mega Gardevoir

blocks.html: Lead: Mega Gardevoir + Togekiss. Mega: Gardevoir. Back: Mamoswine (Scarf), Houndoom (Life Orb, Flash Fire), Garchomp (Life Orb), Metagross.
Damage you can count on:

cells: 96 to 113% with Life Orb; less with Leftovers

blocks.html: Turn by turn

items.html: Turn 1 (leads Mega Salamence + Hitmontop): expect Fake Out from Hitmontop and Double-Edge from Salamence. Togekiss uses Follow Me: both single-target attacks, Fake Out included, go into Togekiss. Gardevoir Mega Evolves and Hyper Voices: Mega Salamence dies (103 to 122%; Intimidate doesn't affect special moves) and Hitmontop takes 2x. If Hitmontop uses Wide Guard instead, Hyper Voice is blocked. Next turn Gardevoir Psyshocks Hitmontop (OHKO) to remove Wide Guard for good, while Togekiss keeps Follow Me up. If Togekiss gets flinched or goes down, switch Gardevoir to Metagross on the next Double-Edge (it resists Flying).
Kill Hitmontop early. It removes Wide Guard, Fake Out and Helping Hand, and stops it re-Intimidating by switching.
Keep Mamoswine and Garchomp in the back until both Intimidates are spent. Intimidate only hits mons on the field when its user comes in.

Naganadel: Beast Boost raises its highest stat after every KO; if it's max Speed, that's Speed, and then nothing of yours outruns it. Kill it before it gets a KO: Psyshock (OHKO) or Scarf Mamoswine's Icicle Crash (OHKO). Its Sludge Bomb does 83 to 98% to Mega Gardevoir.
Magnezone: Sturdy means it survives any one hit from full. Houndoom's Flamethrower plus any second hit, or Earthquake from Garchomp or Mamoswine when Togekiss is the other mon.
Gastrodon: Mega Gardevoir's Energy Ball (63% OHKO). Its Icy Wind is 4x on Garchomp and slows your side.
Pyroar: Garchomp's Earthquake (OHKO with Togekiss as partner) or Stone Edge. Houndoom's Flash Fire eats its Heat Wave, but Scorching Sands is 2x on Houndoom.

blocks.html: Watch out

items.html: Metagross and Mamoswine are weak to all three Fire users. Naganadel's Heat Wave does 47 to 55% to Metagross. Houndoom is the safe switch-in on a predicted Heat Wave or Flamethrower, and absorbing one powers up its own Fire moves.
Salamence's Rock Slide is 2x on Togekiss and Houndoom.
Pyroar's ability is listed as "Royal roar" in the one source that covers it, which isn't a real ability, so I don't know what it actually runs.

blocks.html: Expect the switch: double battle, so no dodge-an-OHKO switching. Watch for absorbers: Gastrodon's Storm Drain pulls in and absorbs every Water move (and it's immune to Electric), Mega Salamence is immune to Ground, but the AI doesn't switch in for plain immunities, so just don't aim Earthquake at it. Only Magnezone and Pyroar resist your Fairy and Ice attacks, and doubles has no resist-switching, so they only matter if they're already on the field.
Beat Jax and you're Champion. Next chapter: post-game and the 100% checklist.

You're Champion. This chapter is the order to tackle everything else in, the one big post-game boss (Aklove at the Ruins of Void, which unlocks New Game+ on a normal file), every post-game mission, the legendary hunt, the Pokédex and the last collectibles. The full lists are in the appendices; this is the plan.

items.html: Mystery Gift codes. The green deliveryman on 2F of any Pokémon Center works after the League. Redeem them all now (codes are in the appendix): several are Pokédex entries you can't get any other way (Mewtwo, Genesect, Marshadow, Poipole, Meltan), and the Zarude code activates Gen 8 species for the DexNav.

Buy the ADM from Captain Davy at the Seaport City Shipyard (250,000). It's the deep-water diving and mining tool, it's needed for Aklove, Zeraora (Thundercap 4F) and Diancie (KBT Expressway), and unboundwiki says it removes the need for HMs.
Aklove at the Ruins of Void (below), then the Ruins legendaries.
Mission #050 Portal Purge (Professor Log, Frozen Heights): catch everything in the portals. Reward: a Master Ball and the two Borrius starter Mega Stones you don't already have.
Mission HQ milestones: 20 missions gives Type: Null, 45 gives Latios or Latias, 65 gives the Shiny Charm. Get the Shiny Charm before your big breeding and DexNav sessions.
The Pokédex (809 National Dex for Mission #069 and Original Color Magearna).
Battle Frontier for BP, Gold Prints and the Black Card.

blocks.title: Aklove at the Ruins of Void

blocks.html: You bring three: Mega Metagross, Houndoom, Gardevoir. Lead Metagross + Houndoom and put both attacks into Meloetta on turn 1 (Meteor Mash plus Dark Pulse). Then Meteor Mash for Tapu Lele, Tapu Koko and Mega Diancie, Flamethrower for Melmetal, and Gardevoir's Specs Energy Ball for Manaphy before Tail Glow. Protect Houndoom the turn Tapu Koko comes in.
Beating him unlocks New Game+. It's a double battle with Jax as your partner, and you bring three mons.
Getting there: buy the ADM from Captain Davy at the Seaport Shipyard, have HM05 Dive, clear the Claydol maze, then beat a Dynamax Claydol. A Chansey in the east of the room heals you before Aklove.

lead_fields: Jax partners you, so the game only lets you take three. The first three are the plan; the last three are swaps. Swap numbers assume Aklove's legendaries have no bulk investment, since their spreads aren't known.

blocks.html: Turn by turn

items.html: Lead Metagross + Houndoom. Houndoom is immune to Psychic moves and Metagross resists them, which takes the teeth out of Meloetta's and Tapu Lele's main attacks.

Turn 1: Mega Evolve Metagross. Both hit Meloetta: Meteor Mash (90 to 106%) and Dark Pulse (80 to 94%) together kill it in one turn. After the Adrenaline Orb it's faster than both, so expect one +2 Shadow Ball first (79 to 94% on Metagross). Don't give it a second turn. If Meloetta Expanding Forces instead, Houndoom takes nothing and Metagross takes resisted damage. Even better.
Psychic Terrain blocks priority against grounded targets, so Bullet Punch is useless while it's up.
Tapu Lele: Meteor Mash (OHKO). Tapu Koko: Meteor Mash (75% OHKO). Koko's Close Combat OHKOs Houndoom: Protect Houndoom the turn Koko comes in, or kill Koko first.
Mega Diancie: Meteor Mash (OHKO). Magic Bounce reflects status moves. Its Earth Power does 59 to 70% to Metagross; Mystical Fire is absorbed by Houndoom's Flash Fire.
Melmetal: Houndoom's Flamethrower (OHKO). Its High Horsepower is 2x on both your leads (46 to 55% on Metagross), and Double Iron Bash OHKOs Gardevoir, so Gardevoir never comes in while it's up.
Manaphy: kill it before Tail Glow: Gardevoir's Specs Energy Ball. Its Scald is 2x on Houndoom.

blocks.html: I haven't confirmed which mons Jax brings as your partner on Expert (on Difficult it was Staraptor, Magnezone and Golurk). If Magnezone is out, your Earthquakes hit it 4x, so Metagross uses Meteor Mash and Zen Headbutt only.

After Aklove the Ruins become a legendary hub: Raikou and Entei from the portal room (then they roam), Suicune in the beast room with those two in your party, then Lugia and Ho-Oh in the lower basement (unboundwiki: Raikou, Entei and Suicune in your party). The Primarium Z is on B2F near where you fought Aklove.

Expect the switch: double battle, so no dodge-a-KO switching. As far as the sources go, none of Aklove's mons has an absorbing ability (Manaphy's is unclear; if it turns out to be Water Absorb it doesn't matter, since none of your three uses Water). The absorbing works in your favour here: Houndoom's Flash Fire eats Mega Diancie's Mystical Fire. Mega Diancie's Magic Bounce only reflects status moves aimed at it, so Houndoom's Nasty Plot (which targets itself) is unaffected.

blocks.html: Strategy notes:

items.html: #050 Portal Purge: 25 portal Pokémon (Ultra Beasts and legendaries), many at night (the table below has the time for each). Bring False Swipe (TM54, Route 10, east of the top of the waterfall), a sleep or paralysis move, and Dusk or Timer Balls. Solgaleo and Lunala: the Route 12 portal holds whichever one you don't have, so bring the other in your party.

Raikou and Entei (part of #050) roam after you trigger them. Sources disagree on the portal: two say Ruins of Void B1F, the unboundwiki legendary list says the Tomb of Borrius. I don't have verified roamer mechanics for Unbound, so I'm not going to tell you how they behave in battle.

#040 More Than a Game: win 100 Frontier battles (200 BP). #029 Hero of the Hall: enter the Hall of Fame with 18 monotype teams, one per type (1,000 BP and 18 Big Nuggets). That one is the biggest grind in the game; plan your monotype teams around your Pokédex catches.

#084 You Are My Only (Pokémon League; reward Ultranecrozium Z): beat the League with one Pokémon. It isn't tagged post-game, but you'll do it on a League rematch, so it's here. Pick a bulky mon with recovery and a setup move, and bring a full bag.

Battle-heavy missions (Battle Frontier streaks, the Antisis Ring Challenge 100-win streak for the Black Card): use your League six with the held items rebalanced for singles, and the Reddit teambuilding advice in the front matter: bulky pivots, status, and a setup sweeper.

blocks.html: Catching Tips that Apply to all of them:

items.html: False Swipe (TM54, Route 10) to get them to 1 HP, then sleep or paralysis.
Dusk Balls at night and in caves, Timer Balls after turn 10, Quick Balls on turn 1.
Save before each one. I couldn't confirm a respawn rule for Unbound legendaries, so treat every knockout as a reload.

blocks.html: What counts: Mission #069 (Professor Log, Frozen Heights) asks you to register all 809 National Dex species (Bulbasaur to Melmetal). Gen 8 and Hisui species (#810 to #905) are extra. No source says forms count. The mission wording is "register", which I read as caught, not just seen; I couldn't confirm that. Reward: Original Color Magearna.
The awkward ones:

items.html: Mystery Gift only (post-game): Mewtwo, Genesect, Marshadow, Poipole (evolve to Naganadel), Meltan (evolve to Melmetal).
Starters you didn't pick: you started with Beldum, so Larvitar and Gible come post-game at the Shadow Base or the Rival's House.
Egg Lady at Magnolia Café: random eggs including Kanto and Kalos starters, Pidgey, Hoppip, Trapinch, Cacnea, Hippopotas, Pidove, Sewaddle and Sandile.

In-game trades: Hitmontop (Epidimy Town, for Lickitung), Pachirisu (Tarmigan Town, for Manectric), Ducklett (Dresco Town, for Alolan Sandshrew), Lampent (Redwood Village, for Zweilous), Amoonguss and Shiinotic (Vivill Town, for each other).
Day-of-week spawns: Rufflet (Great Desert, Monday), Vullaby (Great Desert, Thursday), Sandygast (Route 3 Mon/Tue, Dehara Beach Wed/Sun), Crabominable (Frozen Forest, Thursday).
Mission #017 Darwin Was Right (evolve 151 Pokémon) gives Mew and Mewnium Z. Do it alongside the Pokédex.

blocks.html: NG+ and the Pokédex. The earlier research said the Pokédex carries over to NG+ except Special Encounters, but the pages that state it were blocked when we checked. Check your Pokédex count at the start of the NG+ file.
The appendices list everything; this is just where to start.

items.html: Zygarde Cells (100): one per row in the appendix, spread across the map. Some need Surf, Rock Climb or the ADM.
Mystery Gift codes (34): all in the appendix. Redeem them with the green deliveryman on 2F of a Pokémon Center after the League.

Mega Stones and Z-Crystals: several are post-game only. Examples: Salamencite (Arthur, Dresco Town), Primarium Z (Ruins of Void B2F), and the Red and Blue Orbs from Vega after you beat him at the Battleground on a Monday, Wednesday or Friday. Each row in the appendix says what it needs.
Costumes (5): appendix.
TMs: the appendix lists all 120 plus the HMs, with locations.

blocks.html: Your Trainer Card turns black at five stars: become Champion, finish all missions, complete the National Dex, win 100 in a row at the Antisis City Ring Challenge, and get every Gold Print at the Battle Frontier (a 50-win streak in every facility). With the Black Card, talk to the Lab assistant in Professor Log's Lab again for the final Stat Scanner upgrade: edit EVs, IVs, gender, level, nature, ability and Hidden Power, and evolve from the menu.

On a normal file the Frontier Card is given at the Battle Frontier gatehouse (entered from Seaport City) after the League. On your NG+ file you carry it over, so the Frontier opens as soon as you reach Seaport City. The full shop and tutor list is in the Battle Frontier section at the end of this chapter.
What BP buys:

items.html: Held items at the Battle Tower middle counter: 16 BP (Adrenaline Orb, Absorb Bulb, Cell Battery), 32 BP (Air Balloon, Blunder Policy, Binding Band), 48 BP (Assault Vest, Black Sludge). The full list with prices is in the held-items appendix.

Move tutors outside the Frontier: northwest corner (Tutors 1 and 2, 4 to 8 BP: Heal Bell, Heavy Slam, Stored Power and more), northeast corner (Tutor 3 at 8 BP: the elemental punches, Iron Head, Zen Headbutt, Drill Run, Air Slash; Tutor 4 at 12 BP: Knock Off, Earth Power, Heat Wave, Hyper Voice, Foul Play and more), and the Pledge and starter-ultimate tutor east of the Battle Mine (4 to 8 BP).
The Stat Scanner Notebook tutor (Mission #013) charges BP prices too.

blocks.html: Team building for streaks: the community advice in the front matter applies doubly here. One fixed team for 50 battles needs bulk, status (Will-O-Wisp, Toxic, Thunder Wave), a speed-control option and recovery, not six glass cannons. Your Gold Prints need a 50-win streak in every facility.
I don't have verified rules for each Frontier facility (format, level, banned Pokémon) or what each Gold Print streak looks like on Expert. Check the facility sign before you commit a team.

chapters.title: Reference: rules, training and team building

blocks.html: The background behind the plans: how Expert's rules work, how to build and train a team for it, full builds for every core Pokémon, and how the boss AI decides when to switch. You don't need to read this to play. Dip in when a plan mentions it.

blocks.title: Expert rules and how they change your approach

cells: You fight every boss at the cap, never above it. Levels can't bail you out, so builds have to.
One over-levelled mon drags the whole boss team up with it. Keep the party level with each other. Regular trainers sit 5 to 7 levels under your highest (Beyond Kanto).
Aces, Experts and every trainer after badge 4 have full EVs in two stats
From Mel onwards an unbuilt mon is simply slower and weaker than its mirror on the other side. Everything you field needs its nature and EVs done first.
You can't potion through a fight. Recovery has to come from moves (Softboiled, Morning Sun, Roost), Leftovers and switching.
Gym field effects hit harder than on Difficult. Beyond Kanto's examples: Crater Town's chip is 1/12 HP per turn, and Polder's rain is heavy rain. Each gym gets a counter-plan in its chapter.
The game expects you to EV train from the first route.
League: no Center, no team changes between fights
Five fights with one six. You can still use the bag and swap held items between rooms. The League team is fixed in advance (see the Your core roster section below).
Boss teams are not randomised on Expert
The rosters in this book are what you will face (Beyond Kanto).

blocks.html: The caps line up with the bosses like this:

cells: Houndoom learns Nasty Plot (54), Gardevoir learns Moonblast (56), Metagross learns Zen Headbutt (56)

blocks.html: Evolution and move levels are from Skeli's tables.
Keep traded or Cloud mons that are above the cap out of your party. One over-cap mon turns the cap off for everyone, and then the bosses scale to it.
What changes in how you Play

items.html: Plan the fight before you walk in. Read the boss page, build the six it asks for, then fight. Walking in with "my team" is how runs die on Expert.
Expect to lose once. The first attempt is scouting. If a turn plan breaks, the "Watch out" notes say what to change.

Kill in one go. Bosses carry healing items and use them when a mon is in KO range. Chip damage that doesn't finish the job is wasted. Set up the kill (hazards, a boost, a burn on the thing hitting you) and then take it.
Your four items are for emergencies, usually one revive and three full heals or status cures. The boss chapters name the four for each fight.
Status and stat drops are worth more than damage early in a fight. An Intimidated, burned physical attacker hits for a third of its normal damage. That is a free setup turn.

blocks.html: This section is built from the community advice you collected: the r/PokemonUnbound "Advanced Teambuilding Guide" for Expert, Insane and the Battle Frontier, and four comments from Expert and Insane players. All of it is paraphrased, then turned into rules for this run. Mechanics are standard Gen 8 unless I say otherwise.

cells: Be ready to change your team for nearly every major fight and to raise mons from scratch. DexNav and Day Care breeding are your best friends. Priority order: EVs, then nature, then IVs.
Every boss page has its own six. When BP or time is short, fix EVs first, nature second, IVs last.
Think in roles and in how team members work together. A combo, such as Toxic Spikes plus a Hex Gengar, is not a whole strategy. Slow teams need Sticky Web or paralysis support.
Each team block in this book gives every mon a role line. If a team has no answer to "what if they're faster than me", it isn't finished.

Don't do Expert with one team. Examples: Infiltrator Crobat for Gym 1, Ribombee for Gym 2, Unaware Quagsire, defensive Gligar or Gliscor, a Stealth Rock Excadrill lead. Add healing, setup and Toxic to movesets. Check Smogon sets for ideas. Trial and error.
The "Community picks" table below says where each of those comes from in Unbound and what it needs. Use Smogon's Gen 8 sets as a starting point, then cut moves you can't get yet.

Clefable is a beast. Clefairy is in the Crater Town Pokémon Center behind the bookcases. Max HP and Defence, Magic Guard, Leftovers, with Moonblast, Stealth Rock, Soft-Boiled and Flamethrower. A great lead: immune to status chip and hazard damage.
Clefable is in your rotating roster with that set. The Unbound Wiki confirms the Clefairy and adds that it holds the Moon Stone you need to evolve it.

blocks.text: The rules, in order of importance

blocks.html: 1. Build each mon around what its base stats already do. The Reddit guide's core point: 252 attack / 252 Speed with a Speed nature is the right spread for a fast, frail attacker, and wrong for most other things.

items.html: Fast attackers (base Speed around 100 or more): 252 Atk or SpA, 252 Spe, Jolly or Timid. On Expert the enemy has perfect stats, so a fast attacker without max Speed, a Speed nature and a perfect Speed IV just loses the tie. Assume any enemy with base Speed over 100 is fully invested.

Slow attackers: if max Speed still doesn't get it past anything that matters, stop paying for Speed. Run 252 HP / 252 Atk with an Attack nature and accept it moves second. Azumarill and Arcanine in your roster are built this way.

Check the matchup in the Pokédex first. If the boss ace has a higher base Speed than your sweeper and you have no Speed control, that sweeper is not your answer to it. The guide's example is Mel's Mega Lopunny (base 135).

Don't build six glass cannons. Priority moves, Tailwind, weather Speed boosts, Trick Room and gym rules (Big Mo's weight rule) all break "I'm faster, so I win". At least two of your six should be able to take a hit.

blocks.html: 2. Spend defensive EVs where they buy the most.

items.html: HP first, in nearly every case, because it helps against both physical and special hits. Then put the rest in the side you expect to be hit on, or split it (the guide's example split is 252 HP / 80 Def / 172 SpD).

EVs matter more on low stats. At your League level of 75, 252 EVs add 47 points to any non-HP stat. On base 50 that is 103 to 150, a 46% jump. On base 150 it is 253 to 300, under 19%. (Calculated with the standard stat formula, 31 IVs, neutral nature.)

So when a mon has huge HP and poor defences, invest in the defences instead of HP. When one defence is already high, shore up the other one: the guide's Gliscor runs 252 HP / 252 SpD because its Defence is fine without help and it wants to stay in to set up.
Specialised walls beat all-rounders if you can predict the attacker. A physical wall and a special wall that switch correctly are each much harder to break than two half-and-half tanks.

blocks.html: 3. Have a plan for Speed in every fight.

cells: Carried (on Ditto). Second one: Crystal Peak 1F, or 48 BP
Move first whatever the Speed stats say
Aqua Jet (Azumarill, Floatzel), Ice Shard (Mamoswine), Extreme Speed (Arcanine), Bullet Punch (Metagross), Sucker Punch (Mawile)
Doubles your side's Speed for four turns
Crobat (relearn), Swanna (Lv 47), or the Frontier tutor (8 BP)
Lowers the Speed of every grounded enemy that switches in
Ribombee, as an egg move (see Community picks)
Luxray's Thunder Wave (Lv 35), TM73 Thunder Wave (mission reward)
Slowest moves first for five turns
TM116, Battle Tower counter, 48 BP. Mainly something bosses do to you
Gyarados learns Dragon Dance at Lv 43

items.html: Priority frees up EVs. A mon whose main attack has priority doesn't need Speed investment, so it can put those EVs into bulk. That is the whole idea of your Azumarill: 252 HP / 252 Atk, and Aqua Jet does the outspeeding.

Know the enemy's Speed control and deny it. If a boss sets Tailwind or Trick Room, your options are: knock out the setter first, Taunt it (TM12, behind the Seaport City Poké Mart), or stall the turns out with Protect (TM17, Fallshore City bazaar, P10,000) and a pivot. Each boss page says which.
Sticky Web does nothing to Flying types or Levitate users, and paralysis can't be put on Electric types. Thunder Wave also can't touch Ground types.

blocks.html: For reference, your League six at Lv 75 with max Speed and a Speed nature (calculated, standard formula):

A fully invested base 100 enemy reaches 247 at Lv 75, base 110 reaches 264, base 130 reaches 297. So Scarf Mamoswine (321) outruns every unboosted mon up to base 130, and Mega Garchomp is slower than unmega Garchomp. Mega stats assume Unbound keeps the official Mega base stats.
4. Carry status moves. Pure attackers stall out. The guide's second half is about this, and every Expert commenter repeats it.

items.html: Burn plus Intimidate deletes a physical attacker. Intimidate cuts Attack to two thirds on entry, a burn halves it again: one third damage. Arcanine does both by itself, then heals with Morning Sun and does it to the next one. A crippled enemy left alive is often worth more than a dead one, because it gives you free turns to set up.
Never burn a Facade or Guts user. The burn makes them stronger. The boss pages flag these.
Will-O-Wisp can't burn Fire types. Toxic can't poison Steel or Poison types. Pick the status that works on the target.

Toxic beats walls that outlast your damage. A bulky mon with Toxic and a recovery move wins slowly against things you can't break. Against a wall that heals and resets your boosts (the guide's example is Tessy's Toxapex with Recover and Haze), status and Taunt work where brute force doesn't.
Taunt shuts down stallers and setup. Encore punishes a predictable setup move.

Frostbite is Unbound's special-side burn: it halves Special Attack. Per the Reddit guide, the reliable sources are Fling with a Snowball and Freeze-Dry (30%, doubled in Hail). Your Alolan Ninetales sets its own Hail and can learn Freeze-Dry as an egg move.
Every defensive mon needs recovery. Softboiled (Togekiss, Clefable), Morning Sun (Arcanine), Roost, Recover, or at least Leftovers. Without it a wall is just a slow attacker.

A status move changes the EVs you want. A Will-O-Wisp user can afford less Defence because it halves what's hitting it, or you can go the other way and make it a dedicated physical wall with both. Decide which job the mon has and build for that one.

blocks.html: 5. Think in roles, not in favourites. A team for a boss fight usually needs most of these:

cells: Sets hazards or weather, or takes the first hit and pivots
Mamoswine (Stealth Rock), Clefable (Stealth Rock, Magic Guard), Arcanine (Intimidate)
Drops physical attackers by switching in
Arcanine, Mawile, Gyarados, Luxray, Scrafty (Hidden Ability)
Burns, paralyses or poisons the threat
Comes in on the thing you can't outspeed
Wins once the enemy is weakened
Azumarill (Belly Drum), Garchomp (Swords Dance), Togekiss and Houndoom (Nasty Plot), Gyarados (Dragon Dance)
Finishes things with priority or a Scarf

blocks.html: A combo is not a team. Toxic Spikes plus Hex is two slots that do one thing; the other four still have to answer the boss's Speed, its ace and its gimmick. When you read a team block, check that each boss mon has a named answer and a named backup.

6. Set up only when it's safe. The guide's examples of boosting sweepers all rely on someone else making room first: a burn, a screen, a slow pivot. In this book that usually means: Intimidate in, burn or paralyse, switch to the sweeper on a weak hit, boost once, then attack. If the boss mon in front of you can still two-hit KO your sweeper, don't boost.

7. Trial and error is part of it. All four commenters say some version of this. Use the plan on the boss page for attempt one. If it fails, change one thing (the lead, one item, one mon) and go again.

blocks.html: Hidden Abilities above are the main-series ones. I have not checked Unbound's ability table for these species, and Unbound does change some abilities. Confirm on the DexNav hover text (it shows the Hidden Ability once you've caught the species) before you grind for one.
Everything here is how you turn a fresh catch into a boss-ready mon. Sources are named per item; where I only have one community comment for something, it says so.

blocks.text: The fast path for a new team member

items.html: Catch it with DexNav once you have a few search levels on the species: better IVs, a shot at the Hidden Ability and egg moves.
Crater Town stall (from Gym 2's town onward): Nature Changer 50 BP, EV Maximizer 50 BP per stat. Two stats and a nature is 150 BP and takes a minute.
Egg Move Tutor in the Move Relearner's house, Crater Town: 15 BP per egg move.
Level it to the cap and teach TMs.
IVs last: a Bottle Cap at the stall if you have one, otherwise leave them until the Frontier opens at Seaport City (Gold Bottle Cap, 200 BP).

blocks.html: Before you reach Crater Town (Rivals 1 and 2, Gym 1), you train EVs by hand with the Macho Brace. Your carried six arrive with their EVs done, so this only affects Beldum and the first catches.

items.html: What it is: a key item that shows any of your Pokémon's full stats, including IVs and EVs, and its movesets (Unbound Wiki). You carry it into NG+.

Upgrade 1 (Notebook, Mission #013): adds four pages you flip with L and R: level-up moves, TM/HM moves, egg moves and move tutor moves. From it you can relearn a forgotten move for a Heart Scale, or buy a Battle Frontier tutor move for BP, anywhere. Unlearnable moves show red, known moves blue (Unbound Wiki).

Why it matters on this run: the Frontier tutor list includes Iron Head, Zen Headbutt, Nasty Plot, Tailwind and Mystical Fire (8 BP each), Hyper Voice, Knock Off, Earth Power and Aqua Tail (12 BP), and Play Rough, Liquidation, Scale Shot, Flare Blitz, Close Combat and High Horsepower (16 BP). If the portable tutor works before you're Champion, most of the "wait for the gem tutor" notes in the builds below stop mattering.

blocks.html: The Frontier tutors themselves are listed as post-game. Whether the scanner's tutor page is usable from the start of NG+ is not confirmed anywhere I could find. Test it in your test start. The builds below assume it is NOT available and name a non-scanner source for every move.

items.html: Upgrade 2 (Black Trainer Card): edits EVs, IVs, nature, ability, level, gender and Hidden Power. See the optional max-out above.

blocks.html: EVs are capped at 252 per stat and 510 in total.
Macho Brace

items.html: Expert gives you a Macho Brace at the start (Beyond Kanto). Put it on whatever you're training.

The upgrade NPC is on Route 10, next to a tree by the southern-most waterfall, south of the Cave of Being. You need Surf. Talking to him the first time gives a free level 2 brace (2x EVs) (Unbound Wiki).

Each upgrade costs Everstones equal to the new level and sets the multiplier to that level: level 3 is 3 Everstones for 3x, up to level 10 for 10 Everstones and 10x. Level 2 to level 10 is 52 Everstones in total (Unbound Wiki).

Everstones: an NPC in Fallshore City gives one when you show a Pokémon that can't evolve; wild Geodude line (5%) and Roggenrola line (10%) hold them (my held-item data). A Reddit commenter adds the mining game.

blocks.html: At 10x, a Pokémon that yields 1 EV gives 10 per knockout, so a stat is maxed in 26 knockouts.

Two loose ends. First, what level the Expert starting brace is, and whether the Route 10 NPC upgrades that one or hands you a second: not stated in any source I read. Second, one Reddit commenter (Scourge_of_Arceus) places the Everstone-for-brace NPC right outside the Crater Town Pokémon Center, not on Route 10. The Unbound Wiki says Route 10. Check Crater Town when you get there; if he's there, you can upgrade long before you have Surf.
Power items

items.html: Each Power item is a mission reward: Power Bracer (Mission #003 A Minor Scrap), Power Belt (#005 Abandonment Issues), Power Anklet (#033 If We Were Meant to Fly), Power Band (#052 Pyukumuku Chucker), Power Weight (#071 The Rogue Electivire). Power Lens is on the ground in Vivill Warehouse B5F, in the room where you fight Aklove.

Upgrade NPC: east of Antisis City, outside Thundercap Mountain. Costs Star Pieces; my data doesn't state amounts. One Reddit commenter says 28 Star Pieces gets a Power item to level 7 and that Star Pieces come from wild Staryu (Good Rod, Dresco and Dehara). Single comment, not checked.
These arrive mid to late game. By then the Crater Town stall has made them mostly redundant. Do the Macho Brace first.

blocks.html: Dresco Town trainer house
A repeatable battle house in Dresco Town with a rotating cast (Unbound Wiki). Every trainer's team is one EV type, which makes it the cleanest EV spot in the early game. Teams are Lv 15.

items.html: The stat for each trainer is from a Reddit comment (Scourge_of_Arceus) and matches the species' main-series EV yields, with one exception: Magby yields Speed in the main games, so Daniel's team is two Sp. Atk and one Speed.
Same comment: the Picnicker and the Psychic only appear after you've reached Blizzard City, and Bram pays the best money.
Party members that share experience also pick up the EVs, so you can train several at once (same comment).
How often each trainer can be re-fought: not stated in my sources.
Bought the wrong EVs? EV-lowering berries (Pomeg, Grepa and the rest) are sold at the Fallshore City bazaar per a Reddit comment, and the EV Maximizer can purge a stat.
Where: by the KBT Expressway entrance in Crater Town (community wikis; confirm on arrival). Gone once you become Champion.
Nature Changer: 50 BP. Resets friendship to 0, so do it before you friendship-evolve something.
EV Maximizer: 50 BP per stat, and can purge a stat.
Bottle Cap Lady: maxes one IV per Bottle Cap, all six per Gold Bottle Cap. She takes caps, not BP.
Egg Move Tutor: in the Move Relearner's house (south of the Pokémon Center), 15 BP per move.

Move Relearner: same house, one Heart Scale per move (Unbound Wiki). This is how evolved mons pick up their "Lv 1" moves: Arcanine's whole kit, Togekiss's Aura Sphere, Clefable's Moonlight, Gardevoir's Dazzling Gleam if you evolve past Lv 29.

blocks.html: Outside NG+ the Nature Changer also lives in a house southwest of the Tehl Town Pokémon Center (Unbound Wiki).
Bottle Caps in your bag don't carry, and the BP shop that sells them only opens at Seaport City. Until then the supply is thin:

items.html: Mission #018 Don't Turn Off the Power (Dresco Town; save the game 100 times): 1 Bottle Cap. Start it as soon as you reach Dresco, you'll hit 100 saves anyway.
Mission #071 The Rogue Electivire (Thundercap Mountain 4F): 1 Gold Bottle Cap, plus the Power Weight, Electirizer and an Elekid egg.
Mission #019 Dowsing Wizard (Tehl Town; find 150 hidden items): 1 Gold Bottle Cap.
Mission #006 All the Right Moves (Polder Town; all 120 TMs): 1 Gold Bottle Cap. Realistically post-game.
Mission #080 Ultimate Pie (Blizzard City, post-game): 3 Gold Bottle Caps.
From Seaport City: Gold Bottle Cap 200 BP, Bottle Cap 50 BP. IV Changer west of Seaport City Port.

blocks.html: The old guide also mentions rare raid drops and KBT mining; I have no drop data for either. So before Seaport, DexNav is your IV tool, and per Forward_Boat's order, IVs are the last thing to worry about.
You carry it into NG+. Details below are from the Unbound Wiki's DexNav mechanics page.

items.html: Set R to DexNav in the settings. Open the DexNav, pick a species from the area list and register it; after that, R scans for it.
You can only search species you've already encountered. A question mark means not yet met.

Signs: rustling grass, a dust cloud in a cave, bubbles on water. Walk, don't run: running can scare it off. Moving far away or pressing B drops the signal. Meeting a different wild Pokémon first also drops it.
Repels don't stop the registered species from appearing, so use them to keep everything else away.
Search level (per species, max 255) goes up every time you meet that species, in wild or trainer battles. Higher search level means it appears more reliably and comes with better odds:

cells: Shows its ability (and held item, once the DexNav is upgraded)
Shows potential IVs. Yellow stars are forced perfect IVs
Egg move chance at its maximum (the wiki describes an increase of up to 80%)

items.html: Hidden Ability odds and the number of perfect IVs both rise with search level. The wiki gives no exact numbers.

Chains: catching or knocking out the registered species builds the chain. Fleeing, or finding one and not engaging it, breaks it. Every 5 in the chain adds a level to the next one (up to +19). The 50th and 100th chain encounters have a 1% shiny chance.
Upgrade: Mission #032 Hunter of the Swamp (Cootes Bog) adds held-item info to the hover text.
What DexNav can't find: Rock Smash encounters, gifts, statics and legendaries. Swarm species only while the swarm is on.
Gen 8 special encounters need a Gen 8 species (#810 to #890) registered, R set to DexNav, and then walking in a valid area until it reports something unusual.

blocks.html: How to use it for a boss mon: when the boss page names a new catch, go to its area, meet the species the normal way a few times to build search level, register it, then chain with Repels on until one shows the ability and star count you want.

items.html: Day Care: Route 5, north of Crater Town. It opens once you've entered Dehara City at least once (Unbound Wiki).

Egg Move Tutor (NG+ only before the credits): Crater Town, 15 BP per move. Use it on every new catch that needs an egg move (Swinub's Icicle Crash, Azurill's Belly Drum and Aqua Jet, Togepi's Nasty Plot).
Egg Move Transfer Tutor: inside the Day Care, P25,000 per transfer, moves an egg move between two Pokémon of the same evolutionary line (Unbound Wiki).
Ditto: wild on Route 5, Route 10, Auburn Waterway and Cube Corp. Mission #009 Armoured Magma (hatch 50 eggs) also gives one.
Destiny Knot: Seaport City Breeding School, or Dehara Game Corner (coin price not in my data). Everstone: see the Macho Brace notes.
Egg Hatcher: house west of the Redwood Village Gym, P12,500 to speed up party eggs. The Egg Buyer in the same house pays P2,000 per egg.
Magma Stone halves egg cycles; Oval Charm gives more eggs. Both carried if you earned them.
Breeding missions worth starting the moment you reach the Seaport Breeder's School: #023 Flaming Body (10 eggs), #009 Armoured Magma (50), #039 Master Incubator (100).

Gems: an NPC in the house behind the Gurun Town Pokémon Center trades any Gem for 20 Hard Stones after the As Hard as They Come mission. Hard Stones come from smashing rocks in the Great Desert and digging in the KBT Expressway. Other gem sources are not in my data; the area chapters note any that turn up.

items.html: Your starter's Mega Stone is in the Shadow Base on 1F, behind the locked door that needs the Level 2 Key Pass, which you get in the main story after Zeph. Any other starter-line stone is a post-game reward (Mission #050 Portal Purge). So a Beldum start gives you Metagrossite mid-game.
With a Beldum start, Gible itself only appears post-game (Shadow Base or the Rival's House). Carrying it is the only way to have Garchomp before the League.
Held Mega Stones are reported to carry on v2.1.1.1. Gible holding Garchompite skips the post-game lock on that one. Result: two Megas before the League instead of one.
Mega Evolution unlocks when you beat Maxima at Tarmigan Mansion (Mega Keystone). The cap then rises to 45, which is exactly when Metang becomes Metagross.

blocks.html: Trade-off: Beldum is dead weight until Metang at Lv 20. It knows Tackle, Flash and Steely Hit (Lv 10). Your carried six handle the early game while it levels.
Fallback: if the test start shows Garchompite did not come across, pick Gible as your starter again so you still get Garchompite at the Shadow Base, and treat Metagross as a post-game project.

items.html: Greninja's ability. Protean is its Hidden Ability and works from Lv 10: every move gets the same-type bonus because Froakie turns into that move's type first (Gen 8 rules in Unbound's engine). Battle Bond is a regular ability in Unbound and turns Greninja into Ash-Greninja after it knocks something out (145 Atk, 153 Sp. Atk, 132 Speed), but it does nothing before Greninja at Lv 36. This guide assumes Protean. Swapping costs 200 BP at the Battle Circus or an Ability Patch on the old save.
Absol's egg moves cover its early game: Bite is Dark STAB until Knock Off at Lv 19, Play Rough is Fairy, and Megahorn is a 120-power Bug move from Lv 10.
Ditto has no egg moves, so I can't tell you what it'll arrive knowing. It only ever has Transform, which the relearner gives back.

Heracross's egg moves fill its early gaps: Revenge is a Fighting move before Brick Break at Lv 30, Rock Blast becomes a five-hit move once it Mega Evolves (Skill Link), and Seismic Toss does damage equal to its level whatever it's fighting.
Growlithe evolves with a Fire Stone at any level. Arcanine relearns everything it skipped (Crunch, Flamethrower, Play Rough, Extreme Speed) at the Move Relearner for Heart Scales.

blocks.text: Your early toolkit: item farming, natures, breeding

blocks.html: The Reddit advice you found is right about the tools; you just don't need carry slots for most of them. The mechanics below are from the engine Unbound is built on (Skeli's Complete FireRed Upgrade source).

items.html: Absol leading = item farming. A Super Luck or Compound Eyes lead changes wild held-item odds from 45% nothing / 50% common item / 5% rare item to 20% / 60% / 20%. The rare slot is four times as likely. Use it for Everstones (Geodude line, Roggenrola line), Big Pearls and a Lucky Egg (Happiny on Route 9, Pelipper, Chansey). Everstones buy evolution stones (4 each at Cube Corp) and Macho Brace upgrades.

Synchronize leading = guaranteed natures. A Synchronize lead gives every wild Pokémon its nature, every time (Gen 8 rules), and gift Pokémon too. Catch Ralts (Route 4) or Abra (Route 7) with Synchronize, set their natures at the Crater Town Nature Changer (50 BP each, once), and keep a Jolly, Adamant, Timid and Modest one in the PC. Swap the right one into the lead slot before you catch a new team member. It saves 50 BP on every mon after that.
Only one lead at a time. Absol and a Synchronize mon both need slot 1, so farm items and catch team members on separate trips.

Breeding. The Day Care is on Route 5 but only opens once you've been to Dehara City (Unbound Wiki). Buy a Destiny Knot at the Dehara Game Corner (500 coins). Ditto holds the Knot; the other parent (caught with the right nature) holds an Everstone. Every egg hatches with that nature and 5 IVs picked from the two parents (the engine passes 5 with a Knot, 3 without). Swap the non-Ditto parent for its best baby each round and you're at 5 or 6 perfect IVs within a few generations, for no BP.

blocks.title: How the AI switches (and how to punish it)

blocks.html: You're right that bosses don't just sit there and eat an OHKO. The switching code in the engine Unbound is built on (Skeli's Complete FireRed Upgrade, public source) spells out exactly when the AI bails. Unbound's own build isn't public, so treat this as very likely rather than certain, and assume every boss uses the smart AI.
When it switches out (single battles):

items.html: To dodge a KO. It predicts the move you're most likely to use. If that move would OHKO its active mon, and its mon wouldn't move first, it looks for a switch-in that either: is immune to your move and outspeeds you or walls you, or walls you: none of your four moves can 2HKO it and its Defence (or Sp. Def) is higher than your Attack (or Sp. Atk), or nothing you have even 3HKOs it. It also has to take less than half its HP from the move you're about to use, or outspeeds you and KOs you, and takes less than half from your move coming in, or would KO you with contact damage (Rough Skin, Rocky Helmet) when you hit it, and survives the hit. If nothing on its bench fits, it stays in and attacks.

To absorb your move. This is checked first, every turn, in singles and doubles. If you're about to use a Fire, Electric, Water or Grass move and a bench mon has the ability that eats it (Flash Fire; Volt Absorb, Lightning Rod, Motor Drive; Water Absorb, Dry Skin, Storm Drain; Sap Sipper), that mon comes in. It won't do it if its active mon can KO you first, or the turn after it already made an absorb switch. Plain type immunities (a Ground type against Electric, Levitate against Ground, a Dark type against Psychic) are not on this list: those only come in through the dodge-a-KO switch.
When it has nothing useful left to click (its attacks can't affect you and it has no useful status move), it switches to something that outspeeds or walls you.
When its Attack, Sp. Atk or accuracy is down to -3, a damage-dealing mon switches out. Three Intimidates force a switch; one or two don't.
It also switches when it's asleep or Yawned, or taking chip like Leech Seed. A mon with Regenerator switches out to heal once it's under half HP and facing a hit that would KO it.

blocks.html: When it won't switch: at 20% HP or less; for about a turn after it has just come in; when Stealth Rock or Spikes would cost the active mon a third of its HP coming back later; when it's faster than you (it thinks it attacks first); and in double battles the dodge-a-KO switch doesn't exist at all (only the absorb and bad-moves switches). Mold Breaker on your attacker also stops absorb switches.
How to Play around it:

items.html: When you have a clean OHKO on a slower mon, look at its bench first. A resist alone isn't enough: the switch-in has to be immune, or survive two hits from every move you have. Your coverage moves are what keep it in. If something there does wall you, expect it to come in, and pick a move that's good on the switch-in or at least neutral on both.

After you KO something, it doesn't send its next mon in party order. It sends whichever scores best against your active mon: something that resists or is immune to your moves, or outspeeds and KOs you. If you're Choice-locked into the move that just got the KO, expect its counter and be ready to switch.
The turn after a switch-in, or when it's low, is your safe turn to go for the KO: it won't switch again.

Speed decides it. If its mon outspeeds you, it attacks instead of switching. Priority moves (Sucker Punch, Ice Shard, Aqua Jet, Bullet Punch, Extreme Speed, Water Shuriken) count as you moving first, so they trigger the switch like anything else.
Hazards keep it in. Stealth Rock hurts most on its Rock-weak mons, which then won't switch out.
Pivot moves (Greninja's U-turn from TM89, Luxray's Volt Switch, Floatzel's Flip Turn) let you answer its switch with your own.
Intimidate cycling can push a physical attacker to -3 and force it out. That resets its drops, so kill it at -2 if you can.

blocks.html: Each gym, Elite Four member and major boss in this guide has an Expect the switch note naming its likely switch-ins for the plan's key hits.

Every big fight follows the same seven parts in the same order: header, boss roster, why it's hard, your team, prep checklist, turn-by-turn plan, watch out and backup. Three kinds of card carry most of the information.

cells: Where, and Single, Double or Multi

Your level cap for the fight. Boss levels scale to your highest mon, so listed levels assume you're at the cap

Sprite box with name and National Dex number, type chips, level, ability, held item, four moves, and a note on what makes it dangerous

cells: Build it exactly like this before the fight

blocks.html: Dragon . On cards they show a Pokémon's typing. In text they

Type chips are the coloured labels like Fire or mark the type of an attack. "2x" and "4x" mean super effective and doubly super effective; "half" and "quarter" are resisted; "immune" means no damage. Every one of those claims in this book was checked against the Gen 6+ type chart. Mel's gym uses Inverse Battle rules and that chapter says so on every line where it matters.

items.html: Tip: an optional improvement.

Note: context.
Unverified: not confirmed, or sources disagree. Check it in game before you rely on it.

blocks.text: Pokemon Unbound 2.1.1.1: what "complete the Pokedex" means

blocks.html: Researched 2026-11-15. Everything here comes from the sources listed at the bottom. Where I could not verify something it says so.

items.html: Borrius (regional) Dex: 498 Pokemon. National Dex: 809 Pokemon (Bulbasaur #001 to Melmetal #809). Source: unboundwiki.com/pokemon/ intro.
The same page says the "true total" in 2.1 is 905 once Gen 8 and Hisui species (#810 to #905) are counted. Those were added as catchable in 2.1 (tvtropes, unboundwiki).
The completion mission counts 809. Gen 8 and Hisui species are extra, not part of the mission requirement as worded by the wiki.

Forms (Alolan, Galarian, Hisuian, Burmy cloaks, Deerling seasons, etc.): no source says forms count as separate entries. The mission is worded as 809 species. Treat forms as optional. Not verified in game.
Mission #069 "The National Pokedex". Given by Professor Log in his lab in Frozen Heights early in the game (listed as a pre-League mission; opens once you have the Pokedex, before Icicle Cave).

Requirement: register all 809 Pokemon. The mission page says you need to capture every one of them. The mission list words it as "register". Whether seen-only entries count is NOT stated anywhere I could read, so assume caught.
Reward: Original Color Magearna, Lv.10.
tvtropes says completing the National Dex is one of the requirements for 100% completion (five stars on the Trainer Card).
No diploma or other item reward was found in any source. Unknown beyond the Magearna.
Related: Mission #017 "Darwin Was Right" (evolve 151 Pokemon) gives Mew and Mewnium Z. Mission HQ milestones: 20 missions = Type: Null, 45 = Latios/Latias, 65 = Shiny Charm.

blocks.html: Per unboundwiki and beyondkanto these only come by Unbound Cloud trade from another CFRU hack. All are Gen 8, so none block the 809 mission:

items.html: Zacian, Zamazenta, Eternatus, Kubfu (and so Urshifu), Glastrier, Spectrier, Calyrex.
Trade-only forms: Hisuian Growlithe, Hisuian Voltorb, Hisuian Qwilfish, Hisuian Sneasel, Hisuian Basculin, Galarian Darumaka (several of their evolutions have post-game Mystery Gift codes instead).

blocks.html: Inside the 1 to 809 range every species has a listed method. The awkward ones:

items.html: Mystery Gift only (post-game, green deliveryman on 2F of any Pokemon Center after beating the League): Mewtwo, Genesect, Marshadow, Poipole (then Naganadel), Meltan (then Melmetal). Codes are in pokedex.csv.
Melmetal: the wiki list flags "Requires Gen 8 Activation".
Starters you did not pick (Larvitar, Beldum, Gible lines): post-game at Shadow Base or the Rival's House.

Egg Lady at Magnolia Cafe hands out random eggs (Kanto and Kalos starters, Pidgey, Hoppip, Trapinch, Cacnea, Hippopotas, Pidove, Sewaddle, Sandile). tvtropes says Froakie eggs are not available until post-game.

In-game trades: Hitmontop (Epidimy Town, for Lickitung), Pachirisu (Tarmigan Town, for Manectric), Ducklett (Dresco Town, for Alolan Sandshrew), Lampent (Redwood Village, for Zweilous), Amoonguss and Shiinotic (Vivill Town, traded for each other), Electrode (Blizzard City, for Onix).
Day-of-week encounters: Rufflet (Great Desert, Monday), Vullaby (Great Desert, Thursday), Sandygast (Route 3 Mon/Tue, Dehara Beach Wed/Sun), Crabominable (Frozen Forest, Thursday).

blocks.text: Gen 8 activation (only matters for #810 to #905 and Galarian forms)

items.html: Redeem the post-game Mystery Gift code for Zarude (3YT4BV7PH4UT), save and reload. After that Gen 8 species start being detected by the DexNav. Needs 2.1.1 or later. Source: PokeCommunity changelog post, emulatorhacks walkthrough.
Some Gen 8 Pokemon are DexNav-only "special encounters" (Regieleki, Regidrago, Enamorus, Morgrem). DexNav is unlocked in Blizzard City after catching or evolving 15 species.
NG+ unlocks after clearing the post-game Ruins of Void story (beating Aklove). Source: PokeCommunity, tvtropes.
The caller's brief says the Pokedex carries over except Special Encounters. I could not open the Miraheze or Fandom NG+ pages (fetch blocked) so that is NOT independently verified here.

Early legendaries on NG+, what I could and could not verify: Zeraora: VERIFIED. unboundwiki species page says the post-game requirement applies "only if not in New Game+"; beyondkanto says it is available before the credits on NG+. Thundercap Mountain 4F, needs the ADM. Diancie: single source (beyondkanto) says Lv.25 on NG+ before the post-game. unboundwiki lists Major Miner (#038) as a post-League mission and says nothing about NG+. Heatran: no NG+ statement found. But its key item (Magma Stone) is the reward of Mission #039 Master Incubator (hatch 100 eggs, needs #009), which is listed pre-League, and the legendary list does not tag Heatran as post-game. So it looks catchable before the League on any file. Inference, not a quoted statement. Volcanion: every source read says "beat the Elite Four again". No NG+ exception found. Unverified. Cosmog: wiki says Vanilla any time, Difficult/Expert/Insane post-game only. No NG+ exception found. Unverified.

Catchable before the League on an NG+ file (by the sources): Hoopa (story), Type: Null and Silvally (20 missions), Latios or Latias (45 missions; 57 of 84 missions are open pre-League per beyondkanto), Zeraora (NG+), probably Heatran (see above), Diancie (single source), possibly the second Lati via Mission #042 and Zygarde via Mission #070 (both pre-League missions, but finishing them pre-League is not confirmed). Everything else is post-game.

pokedex.csv was built from the unboundwiki.com/pokemon/ table (NAT DEX, Location, Method). The table was read through a fetch tool that paraphrases, so wording is condensed. A few evolution levels in the wiki text differ from the main games (Boldore, Palpitoad, Vanillish, Vanilluxe, Klang, Klinklang, Mienshao, Braviary, Barbaracle, Corvisquire); those rows say "source text says". Check in game.

Conflicts found and resolved against the species pages: Zekrom is night (not day), Blacephalon is night, Keldeo is in the Route 17 cave (not Cave of Being), Tapu Koko's portal is on the Route 11 cliffs reached through Cliff Cave.
Unresolved: Raikou/Entei portal is "Ruins of Void" in two sources and "Tomb of Borrius" in the unboundwiki legendary list. Portal Purge is said to cover 25 portal Pokemon.
Overqwil's Mystery Gift code was not captured.
romhackguides.com encounter tables looked incomplete (Route 1 land only, starters missing) so they were not used. nuzlockeredux lists by type without methods; used only as a spot check.
